em_1_minuto.titulo: A blood cancer common in older adults
em_1_minuto.texto: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) is usually diagnosed between ages 65 and 74. In SUS, Brazil's public health system, the first treatment is FCR: chemotherapy with fludarabine and cyclophosphamide plus rituximab.
In a systematic review with meta-analysis, they pooled the two large clinical trials (1,300 patients) that compared ibrutinib plus rituximab (IR) with FCR.

em_1_minuto.titulo: 59% lower risk of the disease progressing
em_1_minuto.texto: With IR, the risk of the disease progressing again fell by 59%. There was no clear difference in overall survival, and safety was similar to FCR.
Conitec, Brazil's health technology agency, has not yet assessed IR as a first treatment. The study gathers the best available evidence for that decision.

secoes.lede: A cancer in which B lymphocytes, the blood's defense cells, slowly build up.

blocos.html:
In chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), small, mature B lymphocytes multiply and build up in the blood, bone marrow, lymph nodes and spleen. It is one of the most common blood cancers in adults: the median age at diagnosis is 69 years.

Early on, it often causes no symptoms and shows up only as a rise in lymphocytes on a blood test. When signs do appear, the most common are enlarged lymph nodes, fever, night sweats, weight loss, fatigue and a shortage of other blood cells.

itens.texto: Fludarabine and cyclophosphamide (chemotherapy) with rituximab (immunotherapy). It is the first treatment for fit patients in SUS.
Ibrutinib, a targeted therapy taken as a pill every day, continuously, with rituximab.

blocos.html: Conitec has already assessed ibrutinib as a second treatment and did not recommend adding it to SUS because of its cost-benefit ratio. The use of IR as a first treatment has not yet been assessed, and that is the gap the study helps fill.

secoes.lede: A systematic review with meta-analysis combines the results of several studies into one, following fixed rules.

itens.texto: The plan was registered in advance in PROSPERO (CRD42023494868) and followed the PRISMA guidelines.
In December 2023, the team searched Medline (PubMed), EMBASE, the Cochrane Library and ClinicalTrials.gov, with no restriction on year or language.
Two researchers chose the studies independently. Of the 1,678 records found, 25 were read in full and 3 papers, from 2 clinical trials, were included.
The results were combined in a random-effects model. Risk of bias was assessed with the RoB 2 tool and certainty of evidence with GRADE.
529 patients (354 with IR and 175 with FCR), up to age 70, mean age 56.7, 67% men. Median follow-up of 5.8 years.
771 patients (386 with IR and 385 with FCR), aged 18 to 75, median age 62, 73% men. Median follow-up of 4.4 years.

secoes.titulo: Less disease progression, with similar safety
secoes.lede: Choose a result to compare the two treatments.

parametros.leitura: Over 5.8 years, 84 of the 354 patients on IR had their disease progress or died, versus 74 of the 175 on FCR.
Over 4.4 years, this happened to 59 of the 386 patients on IR and to 118 of the 385 on FCR: practically half.
A severe drop in neutrophils, defense cells, was much less frequent with IR.
Severe anemia was also less common in the group that received IR.
An expected effect of ibrutinib: severe high blood pressure was more frequent with IR.
Cardiac events also appeared more often with IR, a point of attention when using ibrutinib.

blocos.nota: Percentage of patients. “Disease progressed” = disease progression or death, calculated from the numbers in Table 2 of the paper (events ÷ participants). Severe adverse effects = grade 3 or higher.

itens.texto: HR 0.41 (95% CI: 0.31 to 0.53): IR reduced the risk of disease progression by 59%. Certainty of evidence: moderate.
HR 0.71 (95% CI: 0.33 to 1.49): no statistical difference between the treatments. Certainty: very low.
Similar risk with both treatments (RR 0.88 in E1912 and 0.99 in FLAIR). The studies could not be combined. Certainty: low.
Neither study provided usable quality-of-life data.

blocos.html: The type of disease matters. In patients with unmutated IGHV, who usually have a more aggressive disease, IR was clearly better (HR 0.33). In patients with mutated IGHV, the difference was not significant (HR 0.44; 95% CI: 0.19 to 1.02). In the E1912 trial, IR also reduced the risk of death in the unmutated IGHV group (HR 0.35).

secoes.titulo: What weighs in favor, and what calls for caution
secoes.lede: The benefit is relevant, but the two studies have differences that need to be considered.

blocos.html:
On the European Society for Medical Oncology (ESMO) scale, an HR of 0.70 or lower indicates a relevant clinical benefit, and IR reached that threshold for progression-free survival. A study on patient preferences showed that more time without the disease progressing is the outcome they value most, and that many prefer pills to intravenous drugs.

As far as the authors know, this is the first systematic review to directly compare IR and FCR including the FLAIR trial, published in 2023.

blocos.titulo: Limitations pointed out by the authors
itens: Neither study reported allocation concealment, which lowered the certainty of the evidence.
The patients differed: in the US they were younger (mean 56.7 years) than in the UK (median 62).
The studies used different systems to classify disease stage (Rai and Binet).
Follow-up time differed (70 × 53 months), which prevented combining the safety data.

secoes.titulo: What the study allows us to say
secoes.lede: An effective and safe option for the first treatment of CLL.

blocos.html: IR was more effective than FCR at keeping the disease under control for longer. There was no additional gain in overall survival and no difference in severe effects: IR was at least as safe as FCR. According to the authors, despite the differences between the studies, ibrutinib plus rituximab should be considered an effective and safe option for the first treatment of CLL.
